carb-015.title: The Early Tournaisian Warm Interval
carb-015.text: A brief glaciation at the Devonian–Carboniferous boundary gave way to warmth. In the Early Tournaisian Warm Interval, from 358 to 353 million years ago, global average temperature reached about 22 °C. The tropics sat near 30 °C, while the polar regions were about 1.5 °C. The warmth did not last. From the Early Mississippian, oxygen isotope (delta-18-O) values rose over the long term, a sign that the climate was cooling again.

carb-018.title: Aragonite seas replace calcite seas
carb-018.text:
The chemistry of seawater tilted, and reef builders had to follow. From the early Carboniferous, the magnesium-to-calcium ratio of seawater rose. By the Middle Mississippian, aragonite seas had replaced calcite seas. That ratio matters because it affects the ability of organisms to biomineralize, to build hard parts from dissolved minerals.

The aragonite seas favoured organisms that secreted aragonite. The dominant reef builders were aragonitic sponges and corals. Aragonite reef builders, including algae and sponges, appeared in the Pennsylvanian.

carb-022.title: The Visean Warm Interval
carb-022.text: For a while, the ice almost disappeared. During the Visean Warm Interval, glaciers survived only in the proto-Andes of Bolivia and Argentina and in highlands of Brazil and southwest Africa. Then the climate cooled again. From the late Visean, carbonate production was restricted to depths under about 10 m, which built flat-topped carbonate shelves with steep sides.

carb-031.title: The Ouachita orogeny
carb-031.text:
A slow, oblique collision raised mountains across what is now the southern United States. In the mid-Carboniferous, the South American part of Gondwana struck Laurussia's southern margin at an angle. This was the Ouachita orogeny, a mountain-building event that began in the Late Mississippian.

It was caused by a series of continental collisions between Laurussia, Gondwana and the Armorican terrane assemblage. The uplifted Ouachita Mountains created foreland basins such as the Delaware Basin and fed rivers through the Pennsylvanian and Permian. Together, the Variscan-Alleghanian-Ouachita orogeny formed the Central Pangean Mountains.

carb-034.title: Patagonia meets Gondwana
carb-034.text:
Patagonia's arrival at Gondwana took tens of millions of years. Subduction-related igneous rocks of 330–320 Ma under the North Patagonian Massif show that subduction began in the early Carboniferous and lasted about 20 million years. The landmass first touched Gondwana in the mid-Carboniferous, with broader collision in the early Permian.

Where Patagonia came from is debated. One theory has all of it as an allochthonous landmass, one that arrived from elsewhere, from Gondwana during the Paleozoic. The other holds that only southern Patagonia is allochthonous and Northern Patagonia is autochthonous. Rifting and the breakup of Gondwana in the early Mesozoic later rotated Patagonia on a large scale.

carb-040.title: Arrow Canyon marks the Pennsylvanian
carb-040.text: A single cliff section in Nevada defines where the Pennsylvanian begins. The base of the Pennsylvanian and its Bashkirian Stage is fixed at Arrow Canyon, marked by the first appearance of the conodont Declinognathodus noduliferus. In those days Arrow Canyon lay in a shallow, tropical seaway that stretched from Southern California to Alaska. The boundary also separates two kinds of rock: the lower Mississippian is carbonate-rich, while the upper Pennsylvanian is rich in siliciclastics and coal.

carb-038.title: All modern classes of fungi appear
carb-038.text: By the late Carboniferous, the fungal family tree was complete at the top level. All modern classes of fungi had appeared, as rocks of Pennsylvanian age show. Land fungi then diversified further as plants and animals grew in size and abundance, giving them more to live on.

carb-062.title: The magnetic field stops flipping
carb-062.text:
Earth's magnetic field normally reverses every so often. From about 312 to 262 million years ago, it did not. For more than 50 million years it held reversed polarity, with north and south swapped from today's arrangement. This stretch is the Kiaman superchron, and it spans the late Carboniferous to the late Permian.

A superchron is a polarity interval lasting at least 10 million years. The Cretaceous Normal Superchron is a comparable spell. So is a possible Ordovician one, found so far only in the Moyero river section north of the polar circle in Siberia. The name Kiaman comes from the Australian town of Kiama, where some of the first geological evidence was found in 1925.

carb-065.title: Mazon Creek's ironstone treasures
carb-065.text: Near Morris, Illinois, a large delta turned the dead into stone. Chemicals released by decaying soft tissue changed the surrounding sediment into a siderite concretion, which encased each fossil in ironstone and preserved it in exceptional detail. The beds hold the enigmatic Tullimonstrum, known only from here. Roughly 200 insect species, some gigantic, show that insects already filled their main modern niches as herbivores, detritivores and insectivores. Another source dates this life to about 300 Ma.

carb-067.title: A brief, intense Kasimovian glaciation
carb-067.text: Carbon dioxide fell to 180 ppm, and the planet froze. Early in the Kasimovian, a short but intense glaciation, lasting less than 1 million years, drove CO2 that low. It ended abruptly as CO2 rose quickly to about 600 ppm, which brought a warmer climate. By then wetland forests had been restructured and tree lycopsids lost. The Kasimovian boundary also covers a time of globally low sea level, which left disconformities in many sequences of this age.

carb-072.title: The first diapsid reptiles
carb-072.text:
The reptiles that would inherit the Earth appear in the fossil record around 305 million years ago. The first diapsid reptiles, such as Petrolacosaurus, date to that time. Diapsids are true reptiles, and the common ancestor of all living reptiles was almost certainly a diapsid. By the end of the Carboniferous, amniotes included saurians and araeoscelids among several new groups.

Climate drove the change. Reptiles went through a major evolutionary radiation in response to the drier climate that came before the rainforest collapse. Amphibians, then the dominant vertebrates, fared poorly in that collapse. Reptiles kept diversifying, thanks to the hard-shelled egg and scales, which hold water better.

perm-008.title: Lizards' ancestors part from the archelosaurs
perm-008.text: The family tree of living reptiles forked during the Permian. The lineage of lizards and their kin, the Lepidosauromorpha, is thought to have split from its sister group, Archelosauria. Among modern groups, Lepidosauria is the sister taxon to Archelosauria, which includes turtles, birds and crocodilians. Lepidosauria itself splits into Squamata and Rhynchocephalia. Yet the earliest modern lepidosaurs are known only from the Middle Jurassic, though Megachirella from the Middle Triassic may be a stem-group squamate.

perm-001.title: Aidaralash marks the start of the Permian
perm-001.text: The Permian begins with a tiny fossil. Its start is marked by the first appearance of the conodont Streptognathodus isolatus. The reference section lies in the Aidaralash River valley near Aqtöbe, Kazakhstan. This Aidaralash GSSP, the official boundary marker, sets the Carboniferous-Permian boundary at 298.9 million years ago and the base of the Asselian.

perm-015.title: Patagonia completes its collision
perm-015.text:
Patagonia's collision with Gondwana had begun long before the Permian and outlasted its start. The landmass first touched south-western Gondwana in the mid-Carboniferous. The broader collision came in the early Permian, and deformation and metamorphism from it continued into the Permian.

After the collision came the rifting and eventual breakup of Gondwana in the early Mesozoic, which rotated Patagonia on a large scale. Its origin is still argued. One theory has all of Patagonia arriving from Gondwana as an allochthonous landmass in the Paleozoic. The other holds that Northern Patagonia is autochthonous and only the southern part is allochthonous.

perm-023.title: Dimetrodon appears
perm-023.text: A sail-backed predator ruled Texas about 295 million years ago. The pelycosaur Dimetrodon evolved then and diversified, and its remains occur at Bromacker in Germany and in the Red Beds of Texas. It was probably the top predator of the Red Beds ecosystem, feeding on animals such as the shark Xenacanthus and the amphibians Trimerorhachis and Diplocaulus. The word pelycosaur, traditionally used for Dimetrodon, is now considered obsolete. Terms such as primitive or basal synapsids have replaced it.

perm-028.title: The Dobele crater
perm-028.text: A 4.5 km crater at Dobele, Latvia, records an impact about 290 ± 35 million years ago, in the Cisuralian. You cannot see it. The Dobele crater is not exposed at the surface.

perm-034.title: Mesosaurs and the oldest amniote embryos
perm-034.text: Brazil and Uruguay hold the oldest known evidence of amniotic ontogeny, the development of an embryo inside an egg. The Artinskian Mangrullo Formation is rich in mesosaur fossils and holds the earliest known amniote embryos. It yields several fossil embryos, a hatchling and very small mesosaurids. Mesosaurus fossils also occur in Permian black shales of Brazil's Paraná Basin, alongside Glossopteris coals. In the top layers the sea connection was reestablished, and the mesosaurs disappeared, replaced again by fish and bioturbating organisms. One source calls the Paraná Basin's Irati Formation, famous for its Mesosaurus fauna, Late Permian.

perm-039.title: The Ternovka crater
perm-039.text: Beneath Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine, lies an 11 km scar from the sky. An impact in the Early or Middle Permian, about 280 ± 10 million years ago, left the Ternovka crater. It is buried and not exposed at the surface.

perm-055.title: A cooling recorded in carbon
perm-055.text:
Carbon in Capitanian limestones tells of a cooling world. Marine limestones of that age record a rise in carbon-13, reflecting a cooling of global climate. This cooling may have caused the end-Capitanian extinction of warm-water species such as large fusulinids, alatoconchid bivalves and waagenophyllid rugose corals.

Diversity followed an odd path. Global diversity rose dramatically in the Capitanian, probably as disaster taxa filled empty guilds, then fell again in the Wuchiapingian after the end-Guadalupian event. That mass extinction was associated with ocean anoxia and acidification, and was possibly caused by the volcanic eruptions that produced the Emeishan Traps.

perm-067.title: The last callistophytalean seed ferns
perm-067.text: The last callistophytalean seed ferns left the record in the Wuchiapingian. Callistophytales, whose coal forests had covered South China, lived from the Pennsylvanian to the Permian. They were reproductively more sophisticated than most other Paleozoic seed ferns. They seem to have out-competed and replaced some of those in the coal swamp vegetation during the Late Pennsylvanian and Permian.

perm-066.title: The first gliding vertebrates
perm-066.text:
The first vertebrates to glide were lizard-like reptiles. Weigeltisaurids, with extendable wings like modern gliding lizards, are the oldest known gliding vertebrates. Their worldwide spread shows that tall, thin forests had become widespread by the Late Permian. Their gliding membrane originated on the lower-lateral surface of the body, unlike those of rib-gliding reptiles.

How well they glided has changed with the evidence. A 2011 study found Coelurosauravus a less efficient glider than modern Draco because of its larger body size. A 2025 study found its body mass had been overestimated and that it would have been a relatively efficient glider.

perm-076.title: The Araguainha impact
perm-076.text:
A 40 km crater on the border of Mato Grosso and Goiás, Brazil, may be tied to the worst extinction of all. The Araguainha impact struck where there was probably a shallow sea. It punched through Paleozoic sedimentary units of the Paraná Basin and exposed the underlying Ordovician granite basement.

Its age, 254.7 ± 2.5 million years ago, overlaps the Permian–Triassic boundary, and some suggest the warming it caused helped trigger the extinction. Its estimated energy is insufficient to cause the global mass extinction directly. But the huge local rifting would have released large amounts of oil and gas from the shattered rock.

perm-089.title: The last spiny sharks
perm-089.text:
The spiny sharks outlasted their rivals for a time, then lost the race. The acanthodians, an early class of jawed fishes, became extinct in the Permian–Triassic extinction, about 250 Ma. Their diversity had been low but stable through the Carboniferous and slipped further in the Permian. Competition from bony fishes proved too much for them.

Acanthodians share features with both bony and cartilaginous fish but are more closely related to the cartilaginous fish. They predate sharks, which they gave rise to.

perm-092.title: The last griffinflies
perm-092.text: The largest insects ever known vanished with the Permian. Several Paleozoic insect groups, including the giant griffinflies (protodonates) and palaeodictyopteroids, were extinct by its end. Griffinflies include the late Carboniferous Meganeura monyi and the even larger Permian Meganeuropsis permiana, with wingspans of up to 71 cm. Of the Paleozoic insect groups, only three are known after the extinction, the largest known mass extinction of insects. Because of it, there is only little fossil record of insects, including beetles, from the Lower Triassic.

perm-093.title: The last progymnosperms
perm-093.text: The last progymnosperms lasted until the end of the Permian. These were the Noeggerathiales, rare in European and North American floras but common in Cathaysian Chinese floras. Progymnosperms were woody, spore-bearing plants thought to have given rise to the seed plants. Noeggerathiales are thought to have grown as cycad-like plants with thick unbranched vertical stems, leafless except for a crown of fern-like pinnate leaves at the top.

perm-094.title: The Paleozoic corals vanish
perm-094.text:
The reef builders of the Paleozoic died with the Permian. Rugose and tabulate corals died out in the Permian–Triassic extinction. They had built reefs in the late Paleozoic ocean that almost certainly served as shelter and nurseries for many other species. About 96% of coral and other anthozoan genera were lost.

Rugose corals had been abundant in seas from the Middle Ordovician to the Late Permian. They have a unique arrangement of septa that preserves bilateral symmetry, unlike the fully radial symmetry of tabulate and modern scleractinian corals. The most vulnerable marine organisms were those with calcareous hard parts, low metabolic rates and weak respiratory systems, notably these corals. Afterward the sea had no more blastoids, fusulinid forams, trilobites or rugose corals.

perm-095.title: The last lycopsid swamps
perm-095.text: In one corner of the world, the Carboniferous coal forests lived on. Lycopod and horsetail swamps survived to the end of the Permian only in Cathaysia, equatorial islands that became South China. By then tree lycopsids were rare, marginal plants there, no longer the main coal formers. The collapse of the Carboniferous rainforests had affected equatorial Euramerica but not Cathaysia to the east, which mostly corresponds to modern China. Lyginopterids also survived into the Late Permian in Cathaysia and equatorial east Gondwana.

tria-005.title: Coelacanths and lungfishes enjoy their heyday
tria-005.text: The Great Dying cleared the water, and old fish filled it. Coelacanths had their greatest burst of diversity in the Early Triassic, just after it. Lungfishes were most diverse during the Triassic, and only three genera survive today. The only living non-tetrapod sarcopterygians are two species of coelacanths and six species of lungfishes. Coelacanths of the genus Latimeria still live in the open oceans and retain many primordial features of ancient sarcopterygians, which earned them a reputation as living fossils.

tria-048.title: A third extinction closes the Early Triassic
tria-048.text: Recovery from the Permian disaster was interrupted. A third post-Permian extinction event struck at the Olenekian–Anisian boundary, ending the Early Triassic. Siberian Traps activity has been linked to it, and to later Middle–Late Anisian and Anisian–Ladinian crises. Strata of 247 to 242 Ma, in the early middle Triassic, show the recovery after the mass extinction.

tria-042.title: Dinoflagellates leave their first fossil cysts
tria-042.text: Dinoflagellate fossils, mostly resting cysts, first occur in the mid-Triassic. Chemical markers hint at a presence back to the Early Cambrian. Some dinoflagellates produce these resting stages, called cysts, which occurs in a little more than 10% of the known marine species. Recognition that they can encyst dates to the early 20th century, in biostratigraphic studies of fossil cysts. Their shapes radiated from the Late Triassic through the Middle Jurassic, when they became prominent phytoplankton. Another source places their first appearance in the microplankton at the Carnian pluvial episode.

tria-062.title: Specialist rhynchosaurs spread across the globe
tria-062.text:
A wet spell reshaped the rhynchosaurs. They diversified around 240 Ma, but lines common in the Middle Triassic died out in the Carnian pluvial episode, leaving specialised hyperodapedontines. That episode introduced markedly more humid conditions across the globe, interrupting the otherwise arid climate of the Late Triassic.

The survivors thrived. Hyperodapedontines were widespread and abundant in the late Carnian, giving rhynchosaurs their broadest, global distribution. Yet by cutting rhynchosaurs off from more generalized niches, the episode would have reduced their versatility and increased their long-term vulnerability to extinction.

tria-081.title: Tuatara relatives spread around the world
tria-081.text: Relatives of the living tuatara once covered the world. Rhynchocephalians had spread worldwide by the end of the Carnian, and went on to be the dominant small reptiles of the Jurassic. They reached their highest morphological diversity then, with a wide range of lifestyles. These included the aquatic pleurosaurs, with long snake-like bodies and reduced limbs, and the specialized herbivorous eilenodontines. They disappeared from Asia after the Early Jurassic.

tria-108.title: The last dicynodonts disappear
tria-108.text:
Dicynodonts, among the most successful Permian therapsids, stayed large plant-eaters until they died out at the end of the Triassic. Their last appearance is uncertain: they survived at least into the late Norian or earliest Rhaetian. Another source says the exact extinction date is uncertain too.

The group Anomodontia includes the dicynodonts, a clade of tusked, beaked herbivores, and is the most diverse and long-lived clade of non-cynodont therapsids. A tightly coiled embryo of the dicynodont Lystrosaurus from the Early Triassic of South Africa indicates that they likely laid eggs.

jura-026.title: Pangaea's great monsoon starts to fail
jura-026.text:
The Pangean megamonsoon is the hypothesis that Pangaea had a distinct seasonal reversal of winds, causing extreme transitions between dry and wet periods through the year. It would have led to immensely arid regions in the interior of the supercontinent, with extremely hot days and frigid nights. Those areas would have been nearly uninhabitable to terrestrial ecosystems.

At the start of the Jurassic the megamonsoon began to fall apart as Gondwana and southern Laurasia dried out. It kept weakening through the Jurassic as the continents drifted apart. When Pangaea finally broke apart by the middle Mesozoic, the megamonsoon fell apart completely.

jura-010.title: The first certain ornithischians appear
jura-010.text:
The dinosaurs that would become the plant-eating giants began small. The earliest definitive ornithischians appeared and diversified in the Early Jurassic. They included small basal forms such as Lesothosaurus, the heterodontosaurids and early thyreophorans. Early ornithischians were relatively small, averaging about 1–2 meters in body length, and were bipedal.

Where heterodontosaurids belong is disputed. One view treats them as very early ornithischians like Lesothosaurus, while a 2021 study nested them alongside Pachycephalosauria.

jura-011.title: The Farallon plate dives beneath North America
jura-011.text: As Pangaea broke apart, an ocean plate began to sink under the west. The Farallon plate started subducting beneath western North America in the Early Jurassic. Mountains in Nevada and California kept rising as plate motions pushed North America northward. During its subduction the plate accreted island arcs and terranes to North America, and much of the west is composed of these accreted terranes. Most of the Farallon plate was subducted. Two remnants persist: the Cocos plate under Central America and the Juan de Fuca plate under Washington, Oregon and northern California.

jura-017.title: Dicroidium makes a last stand in Antarctica
jura-017.text: Dicroidium, a seed fern that grew as large trees, was widely distributed and dominant over Gondwana during the Triassic. Its ecosystems collapsed during the end-Triassic mass extinction. The plant clung on only as a relict in Antarctica into the Early Jurassic. The related peltasperm Lepidopteris likewise lingered in Patagonia.

jura-024.title: Seawater flips from aragonite to calcite
jura-024.text: The chemistry of the sea flipped in the Early Jurassic. The world's oceans changed from aragonite-sea to calcite-sea chemistry, favouring the dissolving of aragonite and the precipitating of calcite. A fall in the Mg/Ca ratio of seawater favors calcite over aragonite. Calcite seas bring rapid, widespread formation of carbonate hardgrounds, calcitic ooids and calcite cements, and dissolution of aragonite shells in shallow warm seas.
